fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9:3), says, “See that no one is missing, for I have a great sacrifice for Baal.” Baal is a false god, so this sounds like the biggest religious event of the year. Just keep your eyes on that word "sacrifice," because the text is about to tell us what Jehu is really up to.

Close, but no new building is on the schedule. Baal already has a temple in this story, and the crowd fills it from end to end. Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9:3), says he has “…a great sacrifice for Baal.” Nobody's hiring contractors in this passage.

No statue gets promised here. Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9:3), tells everyone, “…I have a great sacrifice for Baal.” The golden figures that show up later in this passage are the calves at Bethel and Dan, and that's a different matter. This one is all about a sacrifice.
That's what Jehu says: “Whoever is missing will not live.” It's a heavy threat. Keep it in mind, because the text tells us right after that Jehu is acting deceptively.
Land never comes up in Jehu's speech. What he says is, “Whoever is missing will not live.” So the stakes are life itself, not property. That's a serious thing to say.

It's a fair guess, since in most crowds a few people skip the meeting. But the text says all the servants of Baal came, and not a single man stayed away. Remember, Jehu had said, “Whoever is missing will not live.”

That's it, baker. Jehu says, “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.” and the keeper of the wardrobe, the man in charge of the clothing, brings out garments for them. I'd say that's the most organized wardrobe department I've ever heard of.

No reading material here, friend. Jehu is talking to the keeper of the wardrobe, and the order is for garments. He says, “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.” Nobody is getting a book club pick. They're getting outfits.

That's right. Jehu tells Baal's servants to look around and see that there are “…no servants of the LORD here among you…” That's the group he names. The check sounds like care for Baal's servants, but the text already told us Jehu is acting deceptively.

Judah never comes up in Jehu's words. He tells Baal's servants, “Look around to see that there are no servants of the LORD here among you…” That's the group he names. Nobody from out of town is mentioned.

No traveling salespeople on this guest list, and Tyre never comes up in Jehu's words. He says to Baal's servants, “Look around to see that there are no servants of the LORD here among you…” That's the group he names.

Yes, eighty. Jehu had stationed eighty men outside the temple, and he gave them a warning about letting anyone escape. So while the servants of Baal are inside making their offerings, those men are posted outside. That's a lot of men on the job.
Twenty is a little low. The text says Jehu stationed eighty men outside. That's four times more than you picked. Twenty would've been a small crew, and Jehu clearly wasn't going small.

Fifty is close, but you're thirty men short. The text says Jehu had stationed eighty men outside. That's a whole extra crew beyond your guess. Somebody had to count all those men, and I'm glad it wasn't me.

This one is true, friend. Jehu tells the guards, “If anyone allows one of the men I am delivering into your hands to escape, he will forfeit his life for theirs.” So the guards have a strong reason to watch the doors. Nobody is going to wander off to check their phone.

The palace isn't where they head. The guards and officers go into the inner room of the temple of Baal. Samaria does come up later in this passage, but not here. Their work at the temple isn't finished yet.
Yes, baker. The text says, “They brought out the sacred pillar of the temple of Baal and burned it.” That's the end of that pillar. It went up in smoke.

That's right. The text says “…he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit…” Jeroboam was an earlier king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). The text names those sins as the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jehu cleaned out Baal, but he did not turn away from this worship.

You'd think a man tearing down temples would keep going. But the text says “…he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit…” Jeroboam was an earlier king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). Those sins are the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and Jehu does not turn away from them.

Moving day isn't mentioned anywhere here. The text says “…he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit…” Jeroboam was an earlier king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). What the text names is the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and Jehu does not turn away from it.

Jehonadab son of Rechab shows up earlier in this passage, but the promise isn't about his family. The LORD says, “…four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” The word "your" means Jehu's own sons. Jehonadab doesn't get this one.

That's right. The text says, “In those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel.” The next verses tell how Hazael, king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), defeated the Israelites throughout their territory. So Israel starts getting smaller.

Doubling would be great news, but the text goes the other way. It says the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel. Hazael, king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), defeats the Israelites in the verses that follow. Israel is shrinking, not growing.

Nobody is pulling out a tape measure here. The text says the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel. Hazael, king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), defeats the Israelites throughout their territory. This is about land getting smaller, not land getting measured.
Hazael, king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), is the one who defeated the Israelites in Jehu's days. He isn't the one who takes Jehu's throne. The text says Jehu's son Jehoahaz reigned in his place.
Jehonadab walked into the temple of Baal beside Jehu (2 Kings 10:23). He still doesn't get the throne. The text says Jehu's son Jehoahaz reigned in his place. The crown stays in the family.
That's right. The text says the duration of Jehu's reign over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years. That's a long stretch on the throne. Nearly three decades of the same king.

Forty is a nice round number, and I respect the confidence. But it's twelve years too high. The text says the duration of Jehu's reign over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years. Twenty-eight is still plenty of time on a throne.
